where: Section 1, bullets on the foreseeing of a change point, and Worked example 1 / Figure
problem: The book says the FS station is marked as a change point, and the bullet list tells the student to 'mark that station as a change point'. In the worked example and the figure, B is an FS taken with no later backsight, so no instrument move follows; calling B a change point contradicts the definition given in Section 3 ('a station read as an FS, then as a new BS').
fix: Say: the FS is the last reading before the instrument moves; that station becomes a change point only when a new BS is taken on it. In the example, B is the closing FS and no change point occurs.

problem: 'If the next reading is smaller, the ground rose: the line of sight sits lower above the ground' is easily misread, because the line of sight itself does not move during a set-up. What is smaller is the height of that line above the staff zero.
fix: Write: 'If the next reading is smaller, the ground rose; the line of sight is then a smaller height above the ground at that station.'

problem: 'This method shows the exact line where a wrong entry was made' overstates what the check does. The arithmetic checks catch addition and reduction slips and locate the page line where the imbalance first appears; they cannot detect a wrongly read or wrongly booked staff reading, because any set of readings will still balance.
fix: Write: 'This method shows the exact line where an arithmetic slip enters the reduction. It cannot detect a wrong staff reading, which satisfies the check but gives wrong levels.'

problem: The lead promises 'two arithmetic checks', but the chapter teaches a single three-part check line (ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL) applied to the same book.
fix: Write 'the arithmetic check' or 'the column checks' instead of 'two arithmetic checks'.
